result.note: Tests the India–EU FTA steel quota, the EU's July 2026 steel regime and the carbon levy and CCTS recognition issue.

questions.prompt: Consider the following statements about steel trade under the draft India–EU Free Trade Agreement published in September 2026:
items: India would receive annual steel quota access of approximately 1.64 million tonnes.
The EU's new steel regime, introduced in July 2026, reserves half its import quota for free-trade partners.
Steel shipments exceeding applicable quotas face a 25% additional duty.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explain: Shipments exceeding applicable quotas face a 50% additional duty, not 25%. India's quota splits into roughly 947,000 tonnes under ordinary trading terms and 695,000 tonnes through the agreement.
questions.source: Shipments exceeding applicable quotas face a 50% additional duty.

questions.prompt: With reference to Indian steel exports to the European Union under the draft India–EU Free Trade Agreement, as of September 2026, consider the following statements:
items: Quota access under the agreement exempts Indian steel from the EU's separate carbon levy.
Brussels has recognised India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) for deductions against the carbon levy.
questions.ask: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explain: Quota access leaves the separate carbon levy in place, and India's CCTS had yet to gain recognition from Brussels. The EU already allows deductions for eligible carbon prices paid abroad, so recognition of the CCTS would lower the carbon bill for Indian steel.
questions.source: But Delhi’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) has yet to gain recognition from Brussels.
